                                                                                          LESSON 1
                                     ABNORMAL PSYCHOLOGY

According to William James (1842-1910)” To study the abnormal is the best way of understanding the
normal”.

What is Psychology?
Psychology is the science of behavior it deals with prediction and control of behavior. Psychologists use the
methods of science to investigate and study all kinds of behavior and mental processes say for example the
activity of single nerve cell to social conflicts that take place in complex societies or say from the
development of language in childhood to the major adjustments required in old age.

Why study Psychology?
  • Know thy self
  • To have a clear understanding of your own behavior, personality, attitudes, emotions, cognitions
       and many more things about yourself and others.

What is Abnormal Psychology?
It is a branch or field of Psychology which relates to mental disorders or psychopathology. It involves
studying patterns of thinking and behaving that are maladaptive, disruptive .These disruptive patterns of
thinking and behaving ultimately effects the individual relationship with others.

You may have heard about a number of mental disorders in television talk shows or in dramas or in the
movies. Most of us are even familiar with the names of these mental disorders, such as Depression, Anxiety
disorder, Eating disorder, Schizophrenia, Post traumatic stress disorder, Obsessive Compulsive disorder and
many more.
Abnormal Psychology studies:
    • The symptoms (what the disorders look like?), about
    • The etiology (what causes these disorders),
    • The assessment (how we can measure the disorders)
    • The diagnosis (how we can classify the disorders)
    • The prognosis (the possible outcome of the disorder)
    • The treatment (how we intervene)
    • Social implications (the effects that disorders have on the individual, their family and on the society
        in particular).

         Elaborate the term Abnormal Psychology. (3)

         A segment of psychology that deals with psychopathology and abnormal behavior. The
         term covers a broad range of disorders, from depression to obsession-compulsion to
         sexual deviation and many more. Counselors, clinical psychologists, and psychotherapists
         often work directly in this field.

            •
                                              SR
         How abnormal psychology is different from Clinical Psychology? (3)

         The main differences between abnormal psychology and clinical psychology are:-

                Clinical psychology includes the scientific study and application of psychology
                for the purpose of understanding, preventing, and relieving psychologically-based
                distress or dysfunction. Abnormal psychology is devoted to the study of mental,
                emotional, and behavioral aberrations. It is the branch of psychology concerned
                                  U
                with research into the classification, causation, diagnosis, prevention, and
                treatment of psychological disorders or psychopathology. Its covers a broad
                spectrum of afflictions and includes neuroses, psychoses, personality disorders,
                psycho physiological disorders, organic mental syndromes, and mental
                     V

                retardation.
            •   Clinical psychology may also engage in research, teaching, consultation, forensic
                testimony, and program development and administration. Abnormal psychology
                studies the nature of psychopathology and its causes, and this knowledge is
                applied in clinical psychology to treat patients with psychological disorders.
            •   The field of abnormal psychology may be called psychopathology. Clinical
                psychology is regulated as mental health profession.

                Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder

Depersonalization

• People with this condition feel as though they have become
  separated from their body and are observing themselves from
  outside.

                    Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder

Depersonalization

• This sense of unreality can extend to other sensory experiences
  and behavior (e.g., unreal self).

                  Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder

Derealization

• The feeling that the external world, too, is unreal and strange
  (e.g., individuals or objects are experienced as unreal, fog,
  dream)

               Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
Diagnostic Criteria

A. The presence of persistent or recurrent experiences of
  Depersonalization/Derealization (as mentioned before).

                  Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
Diagnostic Criteria

B. During the depersonalization or derealization experiences,
   reality testing remains intact.

                   Dissociative Disorders
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
Diagnostic Criteria

C. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment
D. Not attributable to or explained by the physiological effects of a
   substance, a neurological or other medical condition, another
   mental disorder.

Specify if :
With Dissociative Fugue:

Other Specified Dissociative Disorders

                Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Psychodynamic theory

• DD are caused by repression, the most basic ego defense
  mechanism:
• people fight off anxiety by unconsciously preventing painful
  memories, thoughts, or impulses from reaching awareness.

                 Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Psychodynamic theory

• Everyone uses repression to a degree,
• but those with dissociative amnesia and dissociative identity
  disorder are thought to repress their memories excessively

                  Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Psychodynamic theory

• DA is a single episode of massive repression. Repressing may be
  his/her only protection from overwhelming anxiety.
• In DID there is continuous use of repression which is motivated by
  traumatic childhood events, particularly abusive parenting

                  Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Behavior theory

• Dissociation grows from normal memory processes such as
  drifting of the mind or forgetting.
• Specifically, they hold that dissociation is a response learned
  through operant conditioning

                    Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Behavioral theory

• People who experience a traumatic event may later find temporary
  relief when their mind drifts to other subjects.
• For some, this momentary forgetting, leads to a drop in anxiety,
  and Increases the likelihood of future forgetting.

                    Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Behavioral theory

• They are reinforced for the act of forgetting and learn—without
  being aware that they are learning—that such acts help them
  escape anxiety.

                    Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Environmental Factors:

•   Traumatic events
•   Physical and sexual abuse
•   Avoidance of emotions experience during an event
•   Adverse childhood experiences

                    Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Personal Factors:

• Harm-avoidant temperament
• Immature defenses
• Cognitive disconnection and over connection schemata

                   Dissociative Disorders
Etiology of Dissociative Disorders
Psychological Factors:

• Severe psychological stresses and Conflicts
